# Preface {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
```

## Why this book exists {.unnumbered}

Asset allocation is taught as a small set of ideas — a frontier, a risk
measure, a constraint, a backtest — and practiced as a long chain of decisions
about data, estimation, solvers and costs, in which the ideas are the shortest
links. The gap between the two is where most of the difficulty lives. A
student who can derive the tangency portfolio on paper is often unable to
produce it from a return matrix, not because the mathematics is hard but
because the implementation asks questions the derivation never did: in excess
of what rate, on which window, under which constraint, with which solver, and
did the solver actually do what it was told.

There is an excellent R package for this work. `PortfolioAnalytics`
[@peterson2026] has been under development for more than a decade, it
supports nine solvers, fourteen constraint types and eleven risk measures, and
almost nobody uses more than a tenth of it — partly because a reference manual
answers *what does this function do* and never *which of these constraints
does my mandate need, and which solver will still honour it once I have added
it*, and partly because several of its defaults are wrong in ways that produce
a plausible answer rather than an error. This book is a course text built on
that package. It states each method in mathematics, attributes it to the
literature, implements it in R on a market whose every property can be
inspected, and then measures how much of the textbook answer survives contact
with data the optimizer had not seen.

The model for how such a book should be built is *Tidy Finance with R*
[@scheuch2023] and *Machine Learning for Factor Investing* [@coqueret2020]:
explain what is being done, state it precisely, cite it, run it, and hand the
reader takeaways and exercises. Where those books end — with a set of factors
and a set of return forecasts — this one begins.

## Who this is for {.unnumbered}

This is a course text, written first for a master's student meeting portfolio
construction in a syllabus. Each chapter is meant to be teachable in one
session: it opens with the question it answers and the work that first asked
it, states the theory with the mathematics in the running text, implements it
with code the student can run on the shipped data, and closes with takeaways
and exercises whose solutions are in @sec-96-solutions. Nothing is assumed
beyond an introductory course in finance and the R of @sec-94-r-primer.

It is also written for a practitioner who knows the theory and wants the
working implementation, including the part the package makes hard. There is
no separate track: the same text carries the derivation for the student and
the callout for the practitioner, because in this subject the two are rarely
far apart. The reader who wants only the machinery can read the
implementation sections and the callouts and skip nothing that matters.

A doctoral student or a researcher is not the reader the prose is aimed at,
but the references are complete enough that the book can be used as a route
into the literature. Every method is attributed on first use, every empirical
claim that the literature has settled carries the paper that settled it, and
the bibliography has been checked entry by entry.

## How the chapters are built {.unnumbered}

Every chapter opens with the question it answers and the work that first asked
it, states what we do, and then moves through theory, implementation and
application. Each closes with key takeaways and exercises; solutions are in
@sec-96-solutions.

Mathematics is in the running text, because a portfolio problem is easier to
read as an optimization problem than as a paragraph. In Parts II to IV we state
the problem and its solution and send the proof to @sec-91-proofs. In Part VIII
we derive in place, because there the theory is the subject.

Where `PortfolioAnalytics` defaults the wrong way, fails silently or accepts a
constraint and then drops it, we say so in a callout placed where the reader
would otherwise walk into it. That material is one of the reasons for this
book, and it is not in any reference manual. Worked examples that the reader
may want to skip on a first pass sit in collapsible boxes.

## How the book is organized {.unnumbered}

The parts follow the allocation hierarchy. Parts II to V work at the level of
asset classes, because a sixteen-asset problem can be seen whole and a
one-hundred-and-eighty-one-asset problem cannot. Part VI then goes inside a
single class and asks which securities to hold. Part VII is about implementing
and evaluating any of it, and Part VIII carries the theory behind the earlier
intuitions.

Running across that hierarchy is a second distinction, between **strategic**
allocation, which sets a long-run policy from unconditional assumptions, and
**tactical** allocation, which departs from that policy using information
available at the time. We define both in @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory
and then say, chapter by chapter, which one is being done. The two ideas are
often run together; they are not the same, and keeping them apart is worth the
small effort it costs.

## The data {.unnumbered}

Every number in the book is computed on a modeled multi-asset market that
ships with the companion package: five regions, sixteen risky asset-class
series, 181 instruments, monthly and weekly over thirty-one model years, all
in dollars, licensed to nobody. It is introduced in
@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market, measured in
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation and documented in full in
@sec-90-data-description. The market is modeled, not recorded — no series is
the history of a real security — and that is what allows the whole
book to reproduce on the reader's machine without an account anywhere. Where a
claim has to be about real markets, the free data reached through the
companion package is used and the chapter says so.

## What you can skip {.unnumbered}

Parts I to VII are the course, and they are complete on their own. Part VIII
gives the theory behind the intuition, the estimators behind the defaults, and
the parts of the literature that have not yet reached the textbooks. Nothing in
the earlier parts depends on it.

## What this book is not {.unnumbered}

It is not an introduction to R, and it is not an introduction to empirical asset
pricing. Where those are needed, they are cited rather than reproduced:

- For getting financial data into R and building factors from it,
  @scheuch2023 is better than anything this book would write, and its companion
  package is used here directly.
- For the machine-learning algorithms behind return prediction, @coqueret2020
  is the reference. This book picks up where the prediction ends.
- For the R language itself, @wickham2023 remains the standard, and
  @sec-94-r-primer offers a short refresher for readers who want one.

## Conventions {.unnumbered}

Vectors are bold lower case, matrices bold capitals, and the symbols are fixed
once in @sec-02-notation-and-data-notation. Returns are simple returns in
decimal, and they enter every optimization in excess of the Treasury bill, for
the reasons given in @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory. Code objects
follow the mathematics: `R` is the return matrix, `Re` the excess-return
matrix, `rf` the bill, `w` a weight vector.

Every chapter runs from the project root, sources one setup file, attaches the
companion package `tidypm`, and loads the data in two lines. The boundary
between the tidy long table the data ship as and the wide matrix the optimizer
wants is crossed explicitly, once per chapter, with `as_xts_pm()`
(@sec-01-setting-up-implementation). Wherever two objects have to line up —
a weight vector and the columns of a return matrix, a group constraint and the
groups it binds — the alignment is asserted in code rather than assumed, and
every figure is built from a single data frame so that no coordinate can be
paired with the wrong label.

Numbers in the prose are computed, never typed. The spelling is American in
the text and follows the package in code, so `ggplot2`'s argument is `colour`.
Functions are set in code font with their parentheses, `optimize.portfolio()`.

## Reproducing this book {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: colophon
#| echo: false
cat("R version:          ", R.version.string, "\n", sep = "")
cat("PortfolioAnalytics: ", as.character(utils::packageVersion("PortfolioAnalytics")),
    "\n", sep = "")
cat("tidypm:             ", as.character(utils::packageVersion("tidypm")), "\n", sep = "")
```

The full dependency set, pinned to the versions this book was built against,
lives in `renv.lock`, and `renv::restore()` recreates it. Every deviation from
the released package versions is listed in @sec-93-package-notes, and
@sec-97-colophon records how the book was built and what has changed.
